detailed_summary.v3.overview: A practical full-day no-cook plan for people without kitchen access. The creator also suggests roasted chana, makhana and dry fruits as backup foods. The package labels the transcript partial, so this result avoids extending beyond the supplied recipes.

title_en.v1.title: Eating Healthier on Indian Streets: Idli, Customized Thali, Roasted Corn, Bhel, Paneer and Light Dinner Options
title_en.v1.reason: These options are clearly evidenced in the transcript.

detailed_summary.v3.overview: The video demonstrates a full day of relatively healthier choices when eating outside. Breakfast centers on idli, with alternatives such as customized aloo paratha, low-oil dosa, bananas with milk or an omelette. Lunch uses a thali customized toward roti, dal, salad and less oily curry, with vegetable biryani, rajma/chole rice and roti-curry as alternatives. Evening options include roasted corn, customized bhel, coconut water, paneer tikka, eggs and soup. Dinner is kept simple with chapati and dal/vegetable curry. Deep-fried and refined-flour-heavy options are generally deprioritized. The most transferable lesson is choosing the better available option and customizing portions/oil rather than expecting perfect food outside.

title_en.v1.title: A Day Eating with an Indian Farmer: Bajra Roti, Raita, Buttermilk, Seasonal Fruit, Early Dinner and Farm Work
title_en.v1.reason: These foods and lifestyle elements are explicitly documented.

detailed_summary.v3.overview: The video follows a Haryana farmer's day from early morning through dinner. The morning meal includes bajra roti, vegetable raita, chutney, butter, buttermilk, pickle and ghee-shakkar, while the farmer performs hours of physically demanding field work. Seasonal guava and sugarcane appear as snacks. Dinner around 5:30 p.m. includes wheat chapatis with methi, aloo-matar and butter, followed later by slowly cooked milk. The creator extracts broader lessons: wake and sleep earlier, prioritize fresh home food, rotate grains and produce seasonally, stay physically active and reduce phone dependence. Some claims—such as ash making roti medicinal, grounding through barefoot walking, sugarcane not spiking glucose, or special benefits of particular milk preparations—are not established by this evidence.

title_en.v1.title: Dinner Foods the Video Says to Limit: Leafy Vegetables, Salads, Sprouts, Curd, Fruit and Heavy Meals
title_en.v1.reason: The transcript clearly names these dinner categories.

detailed_summary.v3.overview: The video recommends a lighter cooked dinner and lists leafy-vegetable curries, raw salads/sprouts, curd, fruits/fruit juice and heavy meals as foods to restrict after sunset. Alternatives include smaller cooked vegetable portions, soups, spiced buttermilk, lentils and khichdi. It also discourages beans, roti plus rice together and combining multiple protein-dense foods at dinner, while advocating an early meal around 7 p.m. The useful general concept is avoiding overeating and choosing a meal that is comfortable before sleep; many specific post-sunset prohibitions are Ayurvedic rules rather than universally necessary dietary restrictions.

title_en.v1.title: If You Must Eat Dinner Late: Light Meals, Mindful Eating, Walking, Vajrasana and a Two-Hour Sleep Gap
title_en.v1.reason: The transcript focuses on strategies for people who cannot eat early.

detailed_summary.v3.overview: The video prefers dinner before sunset but acknowledges that students, shift workers and professionals may need to eat late. Its proposed routine includes ginger with rock salt before dinner, right-nostril breathing, eating without phone/TV distraction, a slow walk or 10–15 minutes of Vajrasana after the meal, at least a two-hour gap before sleep and sleeping on the left side. Among these, keeping dinner lighter, avoiding immediately lying down and allowing time before sleep are the most broadly practical ideas. The video's explanation that food after sunset rots and creates toxins, and its claims that specific breathing or ginger can restore digestive fire, are traditional rather than established mechanisms.
